claim: Local adaptation commonly involves alleles of large effect, which experience fitness advantages when in positive linkage disequilibrium (LD).
source: Local adaptation commonly involves alleles of large effect, which experience fitness advantages when in positive linkage disequilibrium (LD).
evidence: This is a general statement about local adaptation presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Segregating inversions suppress recombination and facilitate the maintenance of LD between locally adapted loci.
source: Because segregating inversions suppress recombination and facilitate the maintenance of LD between locally adapted loci, they are also commonly found to be associated with adaptive divergence.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific understanding about the role of inversions in maintaining linkage disequilibrium.

claim: Inversions are commonly found to be associated with adaptive divergence.
source: Because segregating inversions suppress recombination and facilitate the maintenance of LD between locally adapted loci, they are also commonly found to be associated with adaptive divergence.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about inversions and adaptation.

claim: There is evidence of significant genome-wide repeatability in signatures of association to phenotypes and environments in three sunflower species.
source: We find evidence of significant genome-wide repeatability in signatures of association to phenotypes and environments, which are particularly enriched within regions of the genome harbouring an inversion in one species.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on genome-wide association analyses conducted by the authors.

claim: Signatures of association to phenotypes and environments are particularly enriched within regions of the genome harbouring an inversion in one species.
source: We find evidence of significant genome-wide repeatability in signatures of association to phenotypes and environments, which are particularly enriched within regions of the genome harbouring an inversion in one species.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the authors' analysis of genomic data across species.

claim: Loci within inversions can harbour mutations that make substantial contributions to adaptation without the benefit of recombination suppression in species lacking a segregating inversion.
source: This shows that while inversions may facilitate local adaptation, at least some of the loci can still harbour mutations that make substantial contributions without the benefit of recombination suppression in species lacking a segregating inversion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed repeatability of association signatures in regions corresponding to inversions in other species.

claim: Most of the strongest signatures of association tend to be species-specific.
source: While a large number of genomic regions show evidence of repeated adaptation, most of the strongest signatures of association still tend to be species-specific, indicating substantial genotypic redundancy for local adaptation in these species.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of association signatures across species.

claim: Species-specific signatures of association indicate substantial genotypic redundancy for local adaptation in sunflower species.
source: While a large number of genomic regions show evidence of repeated adaptation, most of the strongest signatures of association still tend to be species-specific, indicating substantial genotypic redundancy for local adaptation in these species.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed species-specific patterns in the data.

claim: FT affects flowering time in numerous plants.
source: The genetic basis of local adaptation is sometimes highly repeatable, with examples of large effect genes driving responses in multiple species, such as FT affecting flowering time in numerous plants (Izawa, 2007; Auge et al., 2019) or Mc1r driving colour polymorphisms in vertebrates (Manceau et al., 2010; Rosenblum et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mc1r drives colour polymorphisms in vertebrates.
source: The genetic basis of local adaptation is sometimes highly repeatable, with examples of large effect genes driving responses in multiple species, such as FT affecting flowering time in numerous plants (Izawa, 2007; Auge et al., 2019) or Mc1r driving colour polymorphisms in vertebrates (Manceau et al., 2010; Rosenblum et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Significant patterns of similar association have been found across many loci for comparisons of conifers.
source: Local adaptation can also be repeated for polygenic traits, with significant patterns of similar association found across many loci for comparisons of conifers (Yeaman et al., 2016), maize and its wild relative teosinte (Tittes et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021), and Brassicaceae (Bohutínská et al., 2021), to name a few.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Significant patterns of similar association have been found across many loci for comparisons of maize and its wild relative teosinte.
source: Local adaptation can also be repeated for polygenic traits, with significant patterns of similar association found across many loci for comparisons of conifers (Yeaman et al., 2016), maize and its wild relative teosinte (Tittes et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021), and Brassicaceae (Bohutínská et al., 2021), to name a few.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Significant patterns of similar association have been found across many loci for comparisons of Brassicaceae.
source: Local adaptation can also be repeated for polygenic traits, with significant patterns of similar association found across many loci for comparisons of conifers (Yeaman et al., 2016), maize and its wild relative teosinte (Tittes et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021), and Brassicaceae (Bohutínská et al., 2021), to name a few.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Genotypic redundancy is a critical factor affecting the repeatability of adaptation.
source: Genotypic redundancy – the potential for many genotypes to yield a given phenotype – is one critical factor affecting the repeatability of adaptation, as high redundancy would be expected to result in lower repeatability (Yeaman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents theoretical understanding.

claim: High genotypic redundancy would be expected to result in lower repeatability of adaptation.
source: Genotypic redundancy – the potential for many genotypes to yield a given phenotype – is one critical factor affecting the repeatability of adaptation, as high redundancy would be expected to result in lower repeatability (Yeaman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation supported by citation.

claim: Shared standing variation is a critical factor affecting repeatability of adaptation.
source: Another critical factor affecting repeatability is shared standing variation, whether present due to introgression or incomplete lineage sorting.
evidence: This reflects established understanding in evolutionary genetics.

claim: Variants shared among lineages are much more likely to contribute to a repeated response than new mutations.
source: In either case, variants shared among lineages are much more likely to contribute to a repeated response than new mutations (MacPherson and Nuismer 2018; Ralph and Coop 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bohutínská et al., 2021 found that repeatability was negatively related to phylogenetic distance.
source: Consistent with this, Bohutínská et al., 2021 found that repeatability was negatively related to phylogenetic distance.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Inversions have been implicated in local adaptation in many species.
source: Inversions have been implicated in local adaptation in many species (Wellenreuther and Bernatchez, 2018), likely due to their effect to suppress recombination among inverted and non-inverted haplotypes, and thereby maintain linkage disequilibrium (LD) among beneficial combinations of locally adapted alleles (Rieseberg, 2001; Noor et al. 2001; Kirkpatrick and Barton, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Inversions suppress recombination among inverted and non-inverted haplotypes.
source: Inversions have been implicated in local adaptation in many species (Wellenreuther and Bernatchez, 2018), likely due to their effect to suppress recombination among inverted and non-inverted haplotypes, and thereby maintain linkage disequilibrium (LD) among beneficial combinations of locally adapted alleles (Rieseberg, 2001; Noor et al. 2001; Kirkpatrick and Barton, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about inversions supported by citations.

claim: Inversions maintain linkage disequilibrium among beneficial combinations of locally adapted alleles.
source: Inversions have been implicated in local adaptation in many species (Wellenreuther and Bernatchez, 2018), likely due to their effect to suppress recombination among inverted and non-inverted haplotypes, and thereby maintain linkage disequilibrium (LD) among beneficial combinations of locally adapted alleles (Rieseberg, 2001; Noor et al. 2001; Kirkpatrick and Barton, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about inversions supported by citations.

claim: Inversions would be expected to preferentially establish and be retained in regions harbouring a high density of loci that can potentially contribute to local adaptation.
source: If there is variation in the density of loci that can potentially contribute to local adaptation, inversions would be expected to preferentially establish and be retained in regions harbouring a high density of such loci (and this expectation would hold for both the capture and accumulation models).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on models of inversion evolution.

claim: Regions with high density of loci contributing to local adaptation would be expected to show stronger signatures of repeated local adaptation.
source: We would also expect to see stronger signatures of repeated local adaptation in such high-density regions.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the logic of inversion evolution.

claim: Helianthus annuus, Helianthus argophyllus, and Helianthus petiolaris harbour large regions of suppressed recombination ('haploblocks'), most of which are inversions.
source: Here, we explore the repeatability of local adaptation in three species of sunflowers, Helianthus annuus, Helianthus argophyllus, and Helianthus petiolaris (Figure 1), which harbour large regions of suppressed recombination ('haploblocks'), most of which are inversions, and are often associated with adaptive traits (Todesco et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Todesco et al., 2020.

claim: Haploblocks in sunflowers are often associated with adaptive traits.
source: Here, we explore the repeatability of local adaptation in three species of sunflowers, Helianthus annuus, Helianthus argophyllus, and Helianthus petiolaris (Figure 1), which harbour large regions of suppressed recombination ('haploblocks'), most of which are inversions, and are often associated with adaptive traits (Todesco et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: H. annuus is the closest wild relative of cultivated sunflower.
source: H. annuus, the common sunflower, is the closest wild relative of cultivated sunflower, which was domesticated from it around 4000 years ago (Blackman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Cultivated sunflower was domesticated from H. annuus around 4000 years ago.
source: H. annuus, the common sunflower, is the closest wild relative of cultivated sunflower, which was domesticated from it around 4000 years ago (Blackman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Populations of H. annuus are distributed throughout the central and western United States.
source: Populations of H. annuus are distributed throughout the central and western United States and generally found on mesic soils, but can grow in a variety of disturbed or extreme habitats, such as semi-desertic or frequently flooded areas, as well as salt marshes.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the species' distribution, likely based on established knowledge.

claim: H. annuus is generally found on mesic soils but can grow in a variety of disturbed or extreme habitats.
source: Populations of H. annuus are distributed throughout the central and western United States and generally found on mesic soils, but can grow in a variety of disturbed or extreme habitats, such as semi-desertic or frequently flooded areas, as well as salt marshes.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the species' habitat preferences, likely based on established knowledge.

claim: H. petiolaris prefers sandier soils.
source: H. petiolaris, the prairie sunflower, prefers sandier soils, and ecotypes of this species are adapted to sand sheets and sand dunes (Ostevik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about habitat preference supported by citation.

claim: Ecotypes of H. petiolaris are adapted to sand sheets and sand dunes.
source: H. petiolaris, the prairie sunflower, prefers sandier soils, and ecotypes of this species are adapted to sand sheets and sand dunes (Ostevik et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: H. petiolaris ssp. petiolaris is commonly found in the southern Great Plains.
source: Here we include samples from two subspecies: H. petiolaris ssp. petiolaris, which is commonly found in the southern Great Plains, and H. petiolaris ssp. fallax, which is limited to more arid regions in Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Arizona (Heiser et al., 1969).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about distribution supported by citation.

claim: H. petiolaris ssp. fallax is limited to more arid regions in Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Arizona.
source: Here we include samples from two subspecies: H. petiolaris ssp. petiolaris, which is commonly found in the southern Great Plains, and H. petiolaris ssp. fallax, which is limited to more arid regions in Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Arizona (Heiser et al., 1969).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about distribution supported by citation.

claim: H. petiolaris and H. annuus have broad and overlapping distributions throughout the central and western United States.
source: H. petiolaris and H. annuus have broad and overlapping distributions throughout the central and western United States and appear to have adapted to similar changes in temperature, moisture, and photoperiod regimes.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about species distributions, likely based on established knowledge.

claim: H. petiolaris and H. annuus appear to have adapted to similar changes in temperature, moisture, and photoperiod regimes.
source: H. petiolaris and H. annuus have broad and overlapping distributions throughout the central and western United States and appear to have adapted to similar changes in temperature, moisture, and photoperiod regimes.
evidence: This is an inference based on their overlapping distributions and ecological characteristics.

claim: H. annuus and H. petiolaris have likely been exchanging genes during much of their history of divergence.
source: There is also evidence indicating H. annuus and H. petiolaris have likely been exchanging genes during much of their history of divergence (Strasburg and Rieseberg, 2008), although partially isolated by strong pre- and post-zygotic barriers (Sambatti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: H. annuus and H. petiolaris are partially isolated by strong pre- and post-zygotic barriers.
source: There is also evidence indicating H. annuus and H. petiolaris have likely been exchanging genes during much of their history of divergence (Strasburg and Rieseberg, 2008), although partially isolated by strong pre- and post-zygotic barriers (Sambatti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: H. argophyllus is found exclusively in the southeast coast of Texas.
source: The third species, H. argophyllus, the silverleaf sunflower, is found exclusively in the southeast coast of Texas and includes both an early flowering ecotype on the coastal barrier islands and a late flowering ecotype inland (Moyers and Rieseberg, 2016; Todesco et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about distribution supported by citations.

claim: H. argophyllus includes both an early flowering ecotype on the coastal barrier islands and a late flowering ecotype inland.
source: The third species, H. argophyllus, the silverleaf sunflower, is found exclusively in the southeast coast of Texas and includes both an early flowering ecotype on the coastal barrier islands and a late flowering ecotype inland (Moyers and Rieseberg, 2016; Todesco et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: H. argophyllus is thought to have undergone cycles of sympatry and allopatry with H. annuus and H. petiolaris over time.
source: H. argophyllus is thought to have undergone cycles of sympatry and allopatry with H. annuus and H. petiolaris over time, but currently only overlaps with H. annuus, with thus overlap likely being a recent event (Heiser, 1951).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: H. argophyllus currently only overlaps with H. annuus.
source: H. argophyllus is thought to have undergone cycles of sympatry and allopatry with H. annuus and H. petiolaris over time, but currently only overlaps with H. annuus, with thus overlap likely being a recent event (Heiser, 1951).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The overlap between H. argophyllus and H. annuus is likely a recent event.
source: H. argophyllus is thought to have undergone cycles of sympatry and allopatry with H. annuus and H. petiolaris over time, but currently only overlaps with H. annuus, with thus overlap likely being a recent event (Heiser, 1951).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The four taxa vary considerably in the breadth of environmental variation spanned by their respective ranges.
source: The four taxa vary considerably in the breadth of environmental variation spanned by their respective ranges, with H. annuus spanning the widest niche and H. argophyllus spanning the narrowest (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: H. annuus spans the widest environmental niche among the four taxa studied.
source: The four taxa vary considerably in the breadth of environmental variation spanned by their respective ranges, with H. annuus spanning the widest niche and H. argophyllus spanning the narrowest (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: H. argophyllus spans the narrowest environmental niche among the four taxa studied.
source: The four taxa vary considerably in the breadth of environmental variation spanned by their respective ranges, with H. annuus spanning the widest niche and H. argophyllus spanning the narrowest (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Strong correlations between phenotype and environment were observed for many combinations, suggesting pronounced local adaptation for some traits.
source: Using the correlation between phenotype and environment as a metric of the strength of local adaptation on individual traits, we observe strong correlations for many combinations (Appendix 1—figure 2), suggesting that local adaptation is quite pronounced for some traits.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of correlations shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The largest values of SIPEC were found for temperature variables.
source: We find the largest values of SIPEC for temperature variables and the smallest values for soil types, and generally find higher values for comparisons between the petiolaris subspecies (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of SIPEC values shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The smallest values of SIPEC were found for soil types.
source: We find the largest values of SIPEC for temperature variables and the smallest values for soil types, and generally find higher values for comparisons between the petiolaris subspecies (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of SIPEC values shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Higher SIPEC values were generally found for comparisons between the petiolaris subspecies.
source: We find the largest values of SIPEC for temperature variables and the smallest values for soil types, and generally find higher values for comparisons between the petiolaris subspecies (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of SIPEC values shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Many windows with signatures of repeated association were revealed by the analysis.
source: This analysis revealed many windows with signatures of repeated association, with the strongest repeated signature found for number of frost-free days (NFFD; Figure 3A; Appendix 1—figure 4), but also showed that many of the windows with the strongest association in one species did not have strong signatures in other species (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on the results of the null-W test shown in Figure 3A and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The strongest repeated signature of association was found for number of frost-free days (NFFD).
source: This analysis revealed many windows with signatures of repeated association, with the strongest repeated signature found for number of frost-free days (NFFD; Figure 3A; Appendix 1—figure 4), but also showed that many of the windows with the strongest association in one species did not have strong signatures in other species (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on the results shown in Figure 3A and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Many of the windows with the strongest association in one species did not have strong signatures in other species.
source: This analysis revealed many windows with signatures of repeated association, with the strongest repeated signature found for number of frost-free days (NFFD; Figure 3A; Appendix 1—figure 4), but also showed that many of the windows with the strongest association in one species did not have strong signatures in other species (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on the results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The proportion of windows classified as WRAs ranged from 6.3 to 44.1% (mean = 14.5%).
source: While we find significantly more WRAs than the 5% expected by chance, ranging from 6.3 to 44.1% (mean = 14.5%; Appendix 1—figure 5), multiple factors can violate the assumptions of this test and increase the proportion of windows classified as WRAs.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis results shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: Significantly more WRAs were found than the 5% expected by chance.
source: While we find significantly more WRAs than the 5% expected by chance, ranging from 6.3 to 44.1% (mean = 14.5%; Appendix 1—figure 5), multiple factors can violate the assumptions of this test and increase the proportion of windows classified as WRAs.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis results shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: Most regions of the genome harbour some shared standing variation between all six pairwise comparisons of the taxa.
source: It is clear that most regions of the genome harbour some shared standing variation between all six pairwise comparisons of the taxa, whether due to segregating ancestral variation or introgression, based on an index quantifying the proportion of shared to non-shared SNPs in each window (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of shared SNPs shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: No consistent differences in the amount of shared standing variation within windows were found when comparing WRAs with the rest of the genome.
source: However, we do not find consistent differences in the amount of shared standing variation within windows when comparing WRAs with the rest of the genome (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The lack of increased shared standing variation in significant windows suggests that introgression is not a primary driver of WRA patterns.
source: Thus, while introgression may make subtle contributions to WRAs, a lack of increased shared standing variation in the significant windows suggests that it is not a primary driver of these patterns.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that WRAs do not show increased shared standing variation.

claim: CRAs varied in number and size across the six pairwise-species comparisons.
source: CRAs varied in number and size across the six pairwise-species comparisons, with particularly large CRAs identified at the sites of known haploblocks (Todesco et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of the CRA analysis results.

claim: Particularly large CRAs were identified at the sites of known haploblocks.
source: CRAs varied in number and size across the six pairwise-species comparisons, with particularly large CRAs identified at the sites of known haploblocks (Todesco et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CRAs in relation to previously identified haploblocks.

claim: For phenotypic associations, CRAs ranged from 168 clusters spanning 48,524,903 bp (1.6% of the genome) in H. argophyllus-H. pet. petiolaris to 1667 clusters spanning 426,409,647 bp (14.2% of the genome) in H. pet. petiolaris-H. pet. fallax.
source: For CRAs identified for phenotypic associations, their extent ranged from 168 clusters spanning 48,524,903 bp (covering only 1.6% of the genome) in H. argophyllus-H. pet. petiolaris to a maximum of 1667 clusters spanning 426,409,647 bp (14.2% of the genome) in H. pet. petiolaris-H. pet. fallax (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on the CRA analysis results shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: CRAs identified for environmental variables tended to be more numerous and cover a larger region of the genome than those for phenotypic associations.
source: CRAs identified for environmental variables tended to be more numerous and cover a larger region of the genome, varying from 1154 clusters comprising 15% of the total genome for H. argophyllus-H. pet. fallax up to 2260 distinct clusters covering 29% of the genome between H. petiolaris subspecies (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This claim is based on the CRA analysis results shown in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: The large extent of the genome covered by CRAs is mainly driven by their occurrence within many different haploblocks.
source: The large extent of the genome covered by CRAs is mainly driven by their occurrence within many different haploblocks, which tend to be unique to each species and cover substantial portions of their genomes (Todesco et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CRA results in relation to haploblocks.

claim: Genes within CRAs tend to be enriched for a large number of GO terms spanning many different categories.
source: Genes within CRAs tend to be enriched for a large number of GO terms spanning many different categories (Appendix 1—figures 9 and 10).
evidence: This claim is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Appendix 1—figures 9 and 10.

claim: Using an approach that corrects for population structure in genotype–environment association tests (BayPass) results in substantially reduced numbers of CRAs.
source: When we use an approach that corrects for population structure in the genotype–environment association tests (BayPass), we find substantially reduced numbers of CRAs (Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results with and without structure correction shown in Appendix 1—figure 11.

claim: The reduction in CRAs with structure correction is likely due to reduced power to detect true positive causal loci when population structure covaries with environment.
source: This reduction is likely due to reduced power to detect true positive causal loci when population structure covaries with environment, as true positives do not 'stand out' relative to the genomic background (Booker et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Environmental variables with a high maximum SIPEC index tended to have a larger number of CRAs.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that environmental variables with a high maximum SIPEC index (i.e. high correlation between environment and some axis of phenotypic variation in both species; Appendix 1—figure 3) also tended to have a larger number of CRAs (Figure 4), with higher repeatability at both the phenotype and genome level for temperature-related variables and much lower repeatability for soil-related variables (with similar patterns for mean SIPEC index; Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: This claim is based on the relationship shown in Figure 4.

claim: Higher repeatability at both the phenotype and genome level was found for temperature-related variables.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that environmental variables with a high maximum SIPEC index (i.e. high correlation between environment and some axis of phenotypic variation in both species; Appendix 1—figure 3) also tended to have a larger number of CRAs (Figure 4), with higher repeatability at both the phenotype and genome level for temperature-related variables and much lower repeatability for soil-related variables (with similar patterns for mean SIPEC index; Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 12.

claim: Much lower repeatability at both the phenotype and genome level was found for soil-related variables.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that environmental variables with a high maximum SIPEC index (i.e. high correlation between environment and some axis of phenotypic variation in both species; Appendix 1—figure 3) also tended to have a larger number of CRAs (Figure 4), with higher repeatability at both the phenotype and genome level for temperature-related variables and much lower repeatability for soil-related variables (with similar patterns for mean SIPEC index; Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 12.

claim: The number of CRAs exhibited a weak negative relationship with the index of standing variation.
source: In all cases, the number of CRAs exhibited a weak negative relationship with the index of standing variation, with environmental variables that had the greatest number of CRAs having the lowest relative amounts of shared standing variation (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 13.

claim: Environmental variables that had the greatest number of CRAs had the lowest relative amounts of shared standing variation.
source: In all cases, the number of CRAs exhibited a weak negative relationship with the index of standing variation, with environmental variables that had the greatest number of CRAs having the lowest relative amounts of shared standing variation (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 13.

claim: The observed similarity in patterns of association among species is not being strongly driven by incomplete lineage sorting or introgression.
source: This suggests that the observed similarity in patterns of association among species is not being strongly driven by incomplete lineage sorting or introgression, as we would expect a positive relationship between the index of shared standing variation and the number of CRAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negative relationship between CRAs and shared standing variation.

claim: For most phenotypes and environments, the proportion of WRAs occurring within haploblocks was much higher than the proportion of non-WRAs occurring within haploblocks.
source: For most phenotypes and environments, we found that the proportion of WRAs occurring within haploblocks was much higher than the proportion of non-WRAs occurring within haploblocks (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is based on the contingency table analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A total of 310 contrasts showed significant enrichment for WRAs in haploblocks compared to only 23 contrasts showing a significantly higher proportion of non-WRAs in haploblocks.
source: Across all species comparisons and environmental/phenotypic variables, a total of 310 contrasts showed significant enrichment for WRAs in haploblocks compared to only 23 contrasts showing a significantly higher proportion of non-WRAs in haploblocks (note that because of non-independence of the phenotypes and environmental variables, there is pseudo-replication inherent in these estimates).
evidence: This claim is based on the statistical analysis of enrichment in haploblocks.

claim: In H. argophyllus, non-WRA top candidates tended to fall within haploblocks less commonly than in the other taxa.
source: In H. argophyllus, while non-WRA top candidates tended to fall within haploblocks less commonly than in the other taxa, WRAs tended to be very strongly enriched within haploblocks (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In H. argophyllus, WRAs tended to be very strongly enriched within haploblocks.
source: In H. argophyllus, while non-WRA top candidates tended to fall within haploblocks less commonly than in the other taxa, WRAs tended to be very strongly enriched within haploblocks (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CRAs were enriched within haploblocks for many traits and environments.
source: As a follow-up, we also tested whether CRAs were enriched within haploblocks (without controlling for whether top candidate windows also tended to be enriched), also finding strongly significant enrichment of CRAs within haploblocks for many traits and environments (Appendix 1—figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 7C and D.

claim: Few significant signatures of enrichment in haploblocks were found for H. petiolaris petiolaris vs. H. petiolaris fallax.
source: It is noteworthy that few significant signatures of enrichment in haploblocks were found for H. petiolaris petiolaris vs. H. petiolaris fallax (Appendix 1—figure 7C and D), perhaps because extensive introgression across non-locally adapted regions of the genome obscures true signal.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 7C and D.

claim: Extensive introgression across non-locally adapted regions of the genome may obscure true signal in H. petiolaris petiolaris vs. H. petiolaris fallax comparisons.
source: It is noteworthy that few significant signatures of enrichment in haploblocks were found for H. petiolaris petiolaris vs. H. petiolaris fallax (Appendix 1—figure 7C and D), perhaps because extensive introgression across non-locally adapted regions of the genome obscures true signal.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: A total of 145 regions were significant for at least one environmental variable or phenotype using PicMin (at FDR < 0.1).
source: After identifying significant windows clustering together those <1 Mbp apart, we found a total of 145 regions that were significant for at least one environmental variable or phenotype (at False Discovery Rate (FDR) < 0.1 applied within each variable).
evidence: This claim is based on the PicMin analysis results.

claim: The largest number of significant regions for environment using PicMin was found with the NFFD variable (20 with FDR < 0.1; 44 with FDR < 0.2).
source: The largest number of significant regions for environment was found with the NFFD variable (20 with FDR < 0.1; 44 with FDR < 0.2) and for phenotypes with total leaf number, a measure of developmental timing of flowering (9 with FDR < 0.1; 19 with FDR < 0.2).
evidence: This claim is based on the PicMin analysis results.

claim: For phenotypes, the largest number of significant regions using PicMin was found with total leaf number (9 with FDR < 0.1; 19 with FDR < 0.2).
source: The largest number of significant regions for environment was found with the NFFD variable (20 with FDR < 0.1; 44 with FDR < 0.2) and for phenotypes with total leaf number, a measure of developmental timing of flowering (9 with FDR < 0.1; 19 with FDR < 0.2).
evidence: This claim is based on the PicMin analysis results.

claim: Of the 720 individual 5000 bp windows with FDR < 0.2 for at least one variable using PicMin, 387 (53.8%) are within 500 bp of a genic region.
source: Considering the 720 individual 5000 bp windows with FDR < 0.2 for at least one variable, 387 (53.8%) are within 500 bp of a genic region, representing a 2.3× enrichment relative to the rate for windows that were not significant hits using PicMin (23.3% of other windows fall within 500 bp of a genic region; Χ2 test p<10–15).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of PicMin results relative to genic regions.

claim: PicMin-significant windows show a 2.3× enrichment for proximity to genic regions relative to non-significant windows.
source: Considering the 720 individual 5000 bp windows with FDR < 0.2 for at least one variable, 387 (53.8%) are within 500 bp of a genic region, representing a 2.3× enrichment relative to the rate for windows that were not significant hits using PicMin (23.3% of other windows fall within 500 bp of a genic region; Χ2 test p<10–15).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of PicMin results.

claim: Estimates of Leff tend to be large, always well over 1000 windows regardless of the trait or environment.
source: We find that estimates of Leff tend to be large, always well over 1000 windows regardless of the trait or environment (Appendix 1—figure 15A).
evidence: This claim is based on the C-score analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 15A.

claim: Even after controls for linkage and assuming a high false-positive rate of 80%, estimates of Leff remain in the hundreds even for the variable with the lowest value of Leff (Eref).
source: Even after controls for linkage and assuming a high false-positive rate of 80%, estimates of Leff remain in the hundreds even for the variable with the lowest value of Leff (Eref; Appendix 1—figure 15C and D).
evidence: This claim is based on the C-score analysis with corrections shown in Appendix 1—figure 15C and D.

claim: Local adaptation in sunflowers is highly flexible, with different species apparently using quite different sets of loci to adapt to the same environment.
source: Taken together, this suggests that local adaptation in these species is highly flexible – different species apparently use quite different sets of loci to adapt to the same environment – yet still involves some component that has minimal redundancy, with inversions playing a particularly important role.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of the overall results.

claim: Local adaptation in sunflowers involves some component that has minimal redundancy, with inversions playing a particularly important role.
source: Taken together, this suggests that local adaptation in these species is highly flexible – different species apparently use quite different sets of loci to adapt to the same environment – yet still involves some component that has minimal redundancy, with inversions playing a particularly important role.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of the overall results.

claim: Homologs of the FT gene were found as significantly repeated loci identified by PicMin.
source: Some of the 'usual suspects' show up in the set of significantly repeated loci identified by PicMin: in addition to the homologs of the FT (FLOWERING LOCUS T) gene reported by Todesco et al., 2020, we also found hits for several other genes involved in circadian regulation and flowering time, including PRR3 (Para et al., 2007), TOE1 (Aukerman and Sakai, 2003), and PHYC (Takano et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2014), which is known to regulate photoperiodic responses in Arabidopsis accessions (Balasubramanian et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on PicMin results and supported by citation to Todesco et al., 2020.

claim: PRR3 was found as a significantly repeated locus identified by PicMin.
source: Some of the 'usual suspects' show up in the set of significantly repeated loci identified by PicMin: in addition to the homologs of the FT (FLOWERING LOCUS T) gene reported by Todesco et al., 2020, we also found hits for several other genes involved in circadian regulation and flowering time, including PRR3 (Para et al., 2007), TOE1 (Aukerman and Sakai, 2003), and PHYC (Takano et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2014), which is known to regulate photoperiodic responses in Arabidopsis accessions (Balasubramanian et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on PicMin results and supported by citation.

evidence: This claim is based on PicMin results and supported by citation.

claim: PHYC is known to regulate photoperiodic responses in Arabidopsis accessions.
source: Some of the 'usual suspects' show up in the set of significantly repeated loci identified by PicMin: in addition to the homologs of the FT (FLOWERING LOCUS T) gene reported by Todesco et al., 2020, we also found hits for several other genes involved in circadian regulation and flowering time, including PRR3 (Para et al., 2007), TOE1 (Aukerman and Sakai, 2003), and PHYC (Takano et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2014), which is known to regulate photoperiodic responses in Arabidopsis accessions (Balasubramanian et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PIN3, ARF4, and MN were found as top hits in PicMin and are involved in plant development and auxin transport.
source: Other top hits included genes involved in plant development and auxin transport (PIN3 [Keuskamp et al., 2010], ARF4 [Pekker et al., 2005], and MN [Bhatia et al., 2016]), and plant immunity (CRK13 [Acharya et al., 2007] and PRR2 [Cheval et al., 2017]).
evidence: This claim is based on PicMin results and supported by citations.

claim: CRK13 and PRR2 were found as top hits in PicMin and are involved in plant immunity.
source: Other top hits included genes involved in plant development and auxin transport (PIN3 [Keuskamp et al., 2010], ARF4 [Pekker et al., 2005], and MN [Bhatia et al., 2016]), and plant immunity (CRK13 [Acharya et al., 2007] and PRR2 [Cheval et al., 2017]).
evidence: This claim is based on PicMin results and supported by citations.

claim: Chromosome 15 harbours a large (72 Mbp) haploblock in H. annuus that is strongly associated with NFFD.
source: As an example, chromosome 15 harbours a large (72 Mbp) haploblock in H. annuus that is strongly associated with NFFD, and also shows some signatures of association in the other taxa, with particularly strong signatures of association on either side of the haploblock in H. argophyllus (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The chromosome 15 haploblock shows some signatures of association in taxa other than H. annuus, with particularly strong signatures on either side of the haploblock in H. argophyllus.
source: As an example, chromosome 15 harbours a large (72 Mbp) haploblock in H. annuus that is strongly associated with NFFD, and also shows some signatures of association in the other taxa, with particularly strong signatures of association on either side of the haploblock in H. argophyllus (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Loci of repeated association identified by PicMin within the chromosome 15 region include CRPK1 and LHY, whose homologs are known to regulate responses to cold.
source: Interestingly, loci of repeated association identified by PicMin within this region include two genes whose homologs are known to regulate responses to cold: COLD-RESPONSIVE PROTEIN KINASE 1,CRPK1 (Liu et al., 2017) and LATE ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL, LHY (Mizoguchi et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on PicMin results and supported by citations.

claim: Strong selection relative to migration is likely acting upon several loci in the chromosome 15 region and in many other regions harbouring inversions.
source: It seems likely that strong selection relative to migration is therefore acting upon several loci in this region, and in many others harbouring inversions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of repeated association.

claim: The observed repeatability associated with inversions supports the local adaptation model as an explanation for the long-term persistence of segregating inversions in sunflower.
source: The observed repeatability associated with inversions further supports the local adaptation model as an explanation for the long-term persistence of segregating inversions (at least in sunflower), rather than mechanisms based on dominance or meiotic drive (Rieseberg, 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models, supported by citation.

claim: The observation of genomic regions harbouring inversions being enriched for WRAs is consistent with the general model for inversion evolution based on local adaptation.
source: Thus, our observation of genomic regions harbouring inversions also being enriched for WRAs is consistent with this general model for inversion evolution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models.

claim: The observations do not provide much insight into whether inversions evolve through the capture or accumulation type of model as either model would be consistent with the results.
source: Unfortunately, our observations do not provide much insight into whether inversions evolve through the capture (e.g. Kirkpatrick and Barton, 2006) or accumulation (e.g. Schaal et al., 2022) type of model as either model would be consistent with our results.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study in distinguishing between theoretical models.

claim: Most of the sunflower inversions are >1 My old and predate any current local adaptation patterns.
source: Most of the sunflower inversions are >1 My old, and therefore predate any current local adaptation patterns, but likely do not predate the genes underlying local adaptation (which appear to be shared among the species we studied).
evidence: This is a statement about the age of inversions, likely based on previous research or inference.

claim: The sunflower inversions likely do not predate the genes underlying local adaptation, which appear to be shared among the species studied.
source: Most of the sunflower inversions are >1 My old, and therefore predate any current local adaptation patterns, but likely do not predate the genes underlying local adaptation (which appear to be shared among the species we studied).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of repeated association.

claim: Only two other studies have documented the involvement of the same loci making contributions in the absence of the recombination-suppressing effect of the inversion.
source: While many studies have demonstrated the importance of inversions for adaptation (Wellenreuther and Bernatchez, 2018; Hager et al., 2022), to our knowledge only two other studies have documented the involvement of the same loci making contributions in the absence of the recombination-suppressing effect of the inversion (Lee et al., 2017; Coughlan and Willis, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Comparative studies of a species lacking an inversion may help identify which genes are driving adaptation in another species with an inversion.
source: This also highlights how comparative studies of a species lacking an inversion may help identify which genes are driving adaptation in another species with an inversion, as segregating inversions tend to have extensive LD that prevents identification of any potential targets of natural selection within them.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of comparative approaches based on the study's findings.

claim: Segregating inversions tend to have extensive LD that prevents identification of potential targets of natural selection within them.
source: This also highlights how comparative studies of a species lacking an inversion may help identify which genes are driving adaptation in another species with an inversion, as segregating inversions tend to have extensive LD that prevents identification of any potential targets of natural selection within them.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of inversions.

claim: Temperature is the strongest driver of repeated adaptation at both the phenotypic and genomic levels in sunflowers.
source: In general, we find that temperature is the strongest driver of repeated adaptation at both the phenotypic and genomic levels.
evidence: This is a summary of the overall findings from the study.

claim: Correlations between traits and home environment tended to be strongest and most similar among species for temperature variables, particularly in comparisons among H. annuus and H. petiolaris subspecies.
source: Across all phenotypes, these correlations tended to be strongest and most similar among species for temperature variables, particularly in comparisons among H. annuus and H. petiolaris subspecies (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The similarity in phenotypic and genomic signatures of repeatability is consistent with an effect of strong selection.
source: The similarity in these phenotypic and genomic signatures is consistent with an effect of strong selection as other artefactual or drift-based explanations for repeatability would not be expected to reflect patterns found at the phenotypic level.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism driving the observed patterns.

claim: The reduced importance of soil variables in the SIPEC index might be partly driven by the fact that all traits were measured on above-ground features.
source: It should be noted that the reduced importance of soil variables in the SIPEC index might be partly driven by the fact that all traits were measured on above-ground features due to the difficulty of getting non-disruptive phenotypic measurements for roots.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential limitation of the study.

claim: Some fraction of the genome contributes to adaptation with low redundancy and high repeatability, which tends to be enriched within genomic regions where there exist inversions in at least one species.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that some fraction of the genome contributes to adaptation with low redundancy and high repeatability (which tends to be enriched within genomic regions where there exist inversions in at least one species), while the remainder of the adaptive response is driven by loci with high redundancy and species-specific contributions.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of the overall results.

claim: The remainder of the adaptive response is driven by loci with high redundancy and species-specific contributions.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that some fraction of the genome contributes to adaptation with low redundancy and high repeatability (which tends to be enriched within genomic regions where there exist inversions in at least one species), while the remainder of the adaptive response is driven by loci with high redundancy and species-specific contributions.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of the overall results.

claim: At least some component of trait variation experiences sufficiently strong selection and has low enough redundancy to drive significant signatures of repeatability above the random null.
source: At least some component of trait variation experiences sufficiently strong selection and has low enough redundancy to drive the significant signatures of repeatability above the random null that we observe here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of repeatability.

claim: Most of the strongest signatures of association are specific to a single species, implying high redundancy for most of the genome.
source: On the other hand, most of the strongest signatures of association are specific to a single species, implying high redundancy for most of the genome, even if there are still some detectable signatures of repeatability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed patterns in the data.

claim: Seed samples were collected from 151 wild sunflower populations covering most of their native distributions during the summer of 2015.
source: Seed samples were collected from 151 wild sunflower populations covering most of their native distributions during the summer of 2015 (H. annuus: 61 populations for GWAS and 71 populations for GEA; H. petiolaris fallax: 23 populations; H. petiolaris petiolaris: 18 populations; and H. argophyllus: 30 populations, Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the data collection methods.

claim: Seeds from 10 additional populations of H. annuus for the GEA analysis had been previously collected in the summer of 2011.
source: Seeds from 10 additional populations of H. annuus for the GEA analysis had been previously collected in the summer of 2011.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection methods.

claim: A total of 39 environmental variables (21 climatic variables, 3 geographic variables, 15 soil variables) were used for the genotype–environment association analysis.
source: A total of 39 environmental variables (21 climatic variables, 3 geographic variables, 15 soil variables; Supplementary file 1) were used for the genotype–environment association analysis (GEA).
evidence: This is a description of the methods and data used.

claim: BayPass version 2.1 was used for genotype-environment association analysis, which explicitly accounts for the covariance structure among population allele frequencies.
source: We used the package BayPass version 2.1 (Gautier, 2015), which provides a re-implementation of the Bayesian hierarchical model, and explicitly accounts for the covariance structure among the population allele frequencies that originate from the shared history of the populations through the estimation of the population covariance matrix.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used, supported by citation.

claim: BayPass renders the identification of SNPs subjected to selection less sensitive to the confounding effect of population demography.
source: This renders the identification of SNPs subjected to selection less sensitive to the confounding effect of population demography (Gunther and Coop, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the properties of the method, supported by citation.

claim: GWAS analysis was performed on 86, 30, and 69 developmental and morphological traits in H. annuus, H. argophyllus, and H. petiolaris, respectively.
source: GWAS analysis was performed on 86, 30, and 69 developmental and morphological traits in H. annuus, H. argophyllus, and H. petiolaris, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methods and data used.

claim: 29 variables were measured in all three focal species and 39 were measured only in H. annuus and in H. petiolaris subspecies.
source: In total, 29 variables were measured in all three focal species and 39 were measured only in H. annuus and in H. petiolaris subspecies (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the data collected.

claim: Seed and flower traits could not be collected for H. argophyllus since most plants of this species flowered very late in the common garden and failed to form fully developed inflorescences and set seeds before temperatures became too low for their survival.
source: Seed and flower traits could not be collected for H. argophyllus since most plants of this species flowered very late in our common garden and failed to form fully developed inflorescences and set seeds before temperatures became too low for their survival.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation in the data collection.

claim: Population structure was controlled for in GWAS by including the first three principal components as covariates and an IBS kinship matrix.
source: Population structure was controlled for in GWAS by including the first three principal components as covariates, as well as an identity-by-state (IBS) kinship matrix calculated by EMMAX (Kang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used, supported by citation.
